name: Degeneracy
definition: The **degeneracy** of a concept class is defined as the degeneracy of its $1$-inclusion graph, i.e. the maximum over induced subgraphs of the minimum degree.
graph_summary: The largest minimum degree among induced subgraphs of the one-inclusion graph.
origin_references: The minimum-degree deletion argument for one-inclusion graphs appears in \cite{haussler1988predicting}; see also the graph-orientation treatment in \cite{alon1992colorings}.
comments: Conditioning gives an induced subgraph of the $1$-inclusion graph, and degeneracy cannot increase on induced subgraphs.

monotonic.proof: The 1-inclusion graph of a subfamily is an induced subgraph of the original graph. Every induced subgraph considered in its degeneracy maximum is also an induced subgraph of the original graph.

c_monotonic.proof: Conditioning gives an induced subgraph of the one-inclusion graph, and graph degeneracy cannot increase under induced subgraphs.

p_monotonic.proof: Counterexample: $\mathcal H=\{01,10\}$ has edgeless one-inclusion graph and degeneracy 0. Projecting to either coordinate gives $\{0,1\}$, whose one-inclusion graph is an edge and has degeneracy 1.

doubly_monotonic.proof: By definition, doubly monotonicity requires both subfamily monotonicity and projection monotonicity; the recorded failure of one of them rules it out.

strictly_monotonic.proof: By definition, strictly monotonicity requires both doubly monotonicity and strict c-monotonicity; the recorded failure of one of them rules it out.
